M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners' Replies to Exceptions                        1 of 10
                                    I.      Introduction and Summary

        On August 20,2026, the Administrative Law Judges ("ALJs") filed the proposal for deci-
sion ("PFD") in this proceeding. And that same day, Commission Counsel set September 2,2026,
as the deadline to file exceptions to the PFD and September 9,2026, as the deadline to file replies
to those exceptions. 1
        In the PFD, "the ALJs recommend selection of Route 894."2 The M31, M32, and M33
Opposition Landowners3 (and 33 other parties) timely filed exceptions to the PFD.4 There, the
M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners supported the PFD generally, filing exceptions only
clarify the M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners' positions on three routes other than Route
894. Now, the M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners timely file replies to four parties'
exceptions regarding the routing issues.5 On those routing issues, the ALJs reached the correct
conclusions in the PFD, which the Commission should adopt in its final order. 6

                                 II.      Routing Criteria (Issues 8-10)

        The M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners agree with the ALJs' recommendation
that the Commission should select Route 894.7 Most of the parties opposing that recommendation

M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners' Replies to Exceptions                                            2 of 10
 in their exceptions support one of the other three "Focus Routes" (Route 296,8 Route 392,9 or
Route 48710). But four parties support either Route 57211 or Route CCG12_two of the poorer
performing "Routes of Interest." 13 According to the ALJs, neither Route 572 nor Route CCG"pre-
sent[sl a clear advantage over the Focus Routes overall such that it should be given serious con-
sideration as the route selected for the Project."14 And the M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Land-
owners agree: Routes 572 and CCG perform worse than Route 894 across the balance of the rout-
ing factors. 15
        Those four parties mostly repeat their arguments from their initial and reply briefs-the
same arguments that the ALJs considered and rejected in the PFD. And none of those four parties
argue in their routing exceptions that the ALJs (1) "did not properly apply or interpret applicable
law, commission rules or policies, or prior administrative decisions"; (2) "issued a finding of fact
that is not supported by a preponderance of the evidence"; or (3) relied on "a commission policy
or a prior administrative decision [thatl is incorrect or should be changed."16 So the Commission
should reject those exceptions to the extent that they recommend Route 572 or Route CCG.

  A.      Carpenter Land and Cattle Co.'s ("Carpenter's") exceptions and Save the Lam-
        pasas' ("STL's") exceptions do not support adopting Route 572 instead of Route 894.

        Neither Carpenter's nor STL's exceptions support modifying the PFD's proposed findings
of fact and conclusions of law to adopt Route 572 instead ofRoute 894.

        1.        Carpenter's exceptions.
        First, Carpenter argues that the PFD improperly relies "solely on a counting of habitable
structures within the notice corridor established by Commission rule" and "urges that the Com-
mission consider all of the routing factors proportionally."17 But the ALJs did just that: the PFD

 comprehensively evaluates each of the statutory and regulatory routing criteria over nearly 50
pages. 18
        Second, Carpenter generally appears to recommend Route 296 instead ofRoute 894.19 But
in the last six pages of Carpenter's exceptions, it begins recommending Route 572 if the Commis-
sion declines to adopt Route 296 because of"its proximity to the Florence ISD school."20 Carpen-
ter did not disagree with the ALJs' determination that "Route 572 is $8.3 million more expensive,
2.5 miles longer, has less paralleling, and impacts 22 more habitable structures than Route 894."21
Instead, Carpenter addresses only Route 572's impact on habitable structures (and does so indi-
rectly) by arguing that "[tlhe Commission must analyze prudent avoidance comprehensively, as
prior Commission practice and the complexity of the issue demand, rather than reduce it to a crude
counting exercise ofhabitable structures."22
        Yet Carpenter's attempt to "analyze prudent avoidance comprehensively" is mostly limited
to participating in the "crude counting exercise of habitable structures" that Carpenter complains
of. Carpenter notes that " [tlhere are multiple habitable structures on Greenwood Creek Ranch that
would be severely impacted if Route 894 were approved" and that a link in Route 296 that runs
near a notable habitable structure (a new elementary school) could be moved slightly further away
from the habitable structure to enhance prudent avoidance. 23 Neither of those points refutes the
ALJs' observation that Route 572 impacts 22 (26%) more habitable structures than Route 894.
        Carpenter also argues that prudent avoidance can be "satisfied even if a route had more
structures estimated within the notice corridor than other routes."24 Although that point is generally
true, 25 it doesn't apply to Route 572, which-instead of limiting exposures to electric and magnetic
fields through reasonable investments of money and effort-increases exposures to electric and
magnetic fields by 22 habitable structures and also increases costs by $ 8 . 3 million . 26

         Carpenter's exceptions do not support overturning the ALJs' determinations that Route 572
doesn't present a clear advantage over Routes 894,487,392, and 296 and shouldn't "be given
serious consideration as the route selected for the Project."27

        2.       STL's exceptions.

        Like Carpenter's position, STL's position appears to be that the Commission should ap-
prove either "Route[I 296 or a hybrid of Route 894 to the east and Route 296 to the West (Route
296 Option A)" because either route "better address the routing factors as opposed to Route 894
when considering all ofthe applicable routing criteria in statute, Commission rules, and Commis-
sion precedent."28 But ten pages into STL's exceptions, STL adds Route 572 as another route that
it supports over Route 894.29 Then STL confusingly concludes by returning to recommending only
"Route 296 or Route 296 Option A."30
        Nowhere in STL's exceptions does STL explain what the ALJs got wrong when they ob-
served that "Route 572 is $8.3 million more expensive, 2.5 miles longer, has less paralleling, and
impacts 22 more habitable structures than Route 894"31 and concluded that Route 572 neither
presents a clear advantage over Routes 894,487,392, and 296 nor "should be given serious con-
sideration as the route selected for the Project."32 Instead, STL ignores Route 572's higher cost
than Route 894.33 And STL fails to address Route 572's longer length and lower rate of parallelling
than Route 894.34 Yet STL somehow claims that Route 572-with its additional 22 habitable struc-
tures- "compares favorably to Route 894 over the issue of prudent avoidance."35
         STL also argues that the PFD (1) "does not adequately address the constraints related to
airports and helipads",36 (2) "fails to give sufficient weight to TPWD's recommendation and the

 impact that Link J22 would have on Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park";37
and (3) ignores STL's flooding concerns, which STL argues that Route 572 better addresses than
Route 894 because Route "572 pass[esl through fewer riparian areas and avoids the [Lampasas
River Watershedl and [Panther Creek Wildlife Management Areal, thereby reducing the concern
about regular flooding."38 None of those three issues support Route 572 or support overturning the
ALJs' routing recommendations regarding Route 572. First, Route 572 impacts seven more avia-
tion facilities (i.e., private airstrips, FAA-registered airports, and heliports) than Route 894 does.39
Second, TPWD "neither intervened nor filed recommendations or informational comments in this
docket."40 So there are no TPWD recommendations that the ALJs allegedly "fail[edi to give suf-
ficient weight to."41 And third, although Route 572 crosses 2.6 miles less riparian areas than Route
894, Route 572 crosses more potential wetlands, more streams, and more lakes or ponds.42 Plus,
Route 572 crosses or parallels the Colorado River and the flashflood-prone San Saba River for an
extra 6.5 miles compared to Route 894.
        Therefore, STL's exceptions, like Carpenter's exceptions, fail to demonstrate that the Com-
mission should overturn the ALJs' determinations that Route 572 doesn't present a clear advantage
over Routes 894,487,392, and 296 and shouldn't "be given serious consideration as the route
selected for the Project."43

 B.      The J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners' exceptions and Cherokee Creek Aligned
         Intervenors' exceptions do not support adopting Route CCG instead of Route 894.

       Neither the J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners' exceptions nor the Cherokee Creek
Aligned Intervenors' exceptions support modifying the PFD's proposed findings of fact and con-
clusions of law to adopt Route CCG instead ofRoute 894.

M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners' Replies to Exceptions                                   6 of 10
          1.       Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors' exceptions.

         The Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors44 assert that Route CCG is either "the best-meets
route" or just "a good route."45 So the Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors complain that "[tlhe
PFD grouped Route CCG among routes that 'received considerably less discussion than the Focus
Routes' and found that none 'present a clear advantage over the Focus Routes overall. „,46 Accord-
ing to them, the "[tlhe ALJs' recommended decision rests principally on a modest cost differential
and a limited habitable-structures comparison, while giving insufficient weight to the full range of
criteria Texas law requires."47
         That's incorrect. In the PFD's nearly 50-page analysis of the routing criteria, the ALJs re-
viewed each statutory and regulatory factor48 and balanced those factors.49 The ALJs highlighted
that "[clompared to any of the Focus Routes, Route CCG is 3.17 miles longer and approximately
$40 million more expensive. Route CCG has 105 habitable structures within 500 feet of the cen-
terline, which is 20 more than Route 894 and nine more than Route 487."50 Further, the ALJs
recognized the expert testimony of Mr. Ryan Hopkins (which rebutted the Cherokee Creek Aligned
Intervenors' single expert witness) who "ranked Route CCG 73rd out of 123 overall" based on Mr.
Hopkins' independent composite scoring analysis of the 122 routes filed in the application plus
Route CCG. 51 Mr. Hopkins' scoring analysis included all the statutory and regulatory criteria, 52
and the Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors didn't dispute Mr. Hopkins' analysis or controvert
his testimony. 53 So it was entirely reasonable for the ALJs to rely on Mr. Hopkins' testimony to

 determine that Route CCG should not "be given serious consideration as the route selected for the
Project."54
        Accordingly, the Cherokee Creek Aligned Intervenors have not demonstrated any grounds
for the Commission to overturn the ALJs' determinations that Route CCG doesn't present a clear
advantage over Routes 894,487,392, and 296 and shouldn't "be given serious consideration as
the route selected for the Project."55

        2.       J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners' exceptions.

        Lastly, the J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners56 don't even argue that Route CCG better
meets the statutory and regulatory criteria than Route 894.57 Instead, they simply contend that
Route CCG is "a reasonable alternative to the Central Corridof' that allegedly "was shown to
better protect the State Parks and other scenic and environmental resources while remaining within
a relatively narrow cost range."58 But the J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners cite nothing in the
record to support those propositions, never explain how Route CCG "better protect[sl" state parks
and other scenic and environmental resources , and avoid mentioning that Route CCG costs S73. 69
million more than Route 894 . 59 The J27 , J25 , J4 Opposition Landowners ' exceptions do not dis -
place (or even conflict with) the ALJs' analysis that "[clompared to any ofthe Focus Routes, Route
CCG is 3.17 miles longer and approximately $40 million more expensive. Route CCG has 105
habitable structures within 500 feet of the centerline, which is 20 more than Route 894 and nine
more than Route 487."60 Thus, the J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners' exceptions cannot support
modifying the PFD's proposed findings offact and conclusions oflaw to adopt Route CCG instead
ofRoute 894.

                                              III.    Conclusion
        For these reasons and in accordance with 16 Texas Administrative Code § 22.262(a), the
M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners respectfully recommend that the Commission should
